nuggets.title: Scanned PDF upload OOMs parser workers

scenario.symptoms: Ingestion queue depth hit 200k after customers bulk-uploaded 400-page scanned PDFs. Parser pods OOMKilled looping retries on the same files.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Parser loads entire PDF into memory with OCR on main thread; no size limits or streaming page pipeline.

incident.headline: Memory-unbounded parsing on huge scanned PDFs

agenda.goal: Parse messy formats well without paying OCR prices for everything.
agenda.opener: Bulk scans killed parser pods—the parsing pipeline is highlighted. How do you make ingestion safe?

evidence.strong: Detects type and routes to layout-aware parsers; keeps headings, reading order and tables (rows with headers); escalates only scanned or complex pages to OCR or vision models; captions figures where needed; strips repeated headers and footers; stores parsed intermediate output; tracks parse-quality signals.
evidence.adequate: OCR for everything or a single generic extractor.

misconceptions.pattern: Runs OCR on every page to be safe.
misconceptions.challenge: Most pages already contain text. What does OCR on five hundred million pages cost?

probes: How do you keep a table usable after parsing?
How would you notice a parser producing garbage?
hints: Use expensive tools only where needed.
Structure matters as much as words.
agenda.referenceFix: Page-streaming OCR, file size and page caps, sandboxed workers with memory limits, dead-letter toxic docs, and async progress to users.

nuggets.title: Concurrent edits create conflicting document versions

scenario.symptoms: Legal team sees two 'latest' versions of the same contract after parallel uploads. Search index shows both as current without merge.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Version ids are client-generated timestamps; server accepts last write without vector clock or content hash dedupe.

agenda.opener: Two versions both marked latest—the versioning path is highlighted. How do you linearize history?

evidence.strong: Every event carries a version; stages reject versions older than the registry's current one; the new version is fully indexed, then marked current, then old chunks deleted, so search never shows a half-indexed document; reconciliation compares sources, registry and indexes.
evidence.adequate: Overwrites on each event without ordering.

misconceptions.pattern: Deletes old chunks before indexing the new version.
misconceptions.challenge: Someone searches during the gap. What do they find?

probes: In what order do you add new chunks and remove old ones?
How do you catch updates whose events were lost?
hints: Swap only once the new version is ready.
agenda.referenceFix: Server-assigned monotonic version, optimistic concurrency tokens, branch conflicts for human merge, content-hash dedupe, and single latest pointer per doc.

nuggets.title: Deletes not propagated to search index

scenario.symptoms: GDPR erasure requests completed in primary store but documents still appear in search results weeks later. Tombstone stream consumer lagging 14 days.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Delete writes tombstone to OLTP but search indexer on separate backlog without SLA; compactor job disabled.

incident.headline: Search indexer lag left deleted docs discoverable

agenda.goal: Meet the strict deletion and revocation deadline.
agenda.opener: Users deleted data but search still finds it—the delete propagation path is highlighted. What's broken?

evidence.strong: Deletes and permission changes take a priority path: mark documents hidden or update ACL metadata immediately (a filter applied at query time), then purge chunks and vectors asynchronously; permission changes are metadata updates without re-embedding; deletion latency is monitored.

misconceptions.pattern: Sends deletes through the same queue as new documents.
misconceptions.challenge: A huge import is queued ahead of the delete. When does the deleted file stop appearing?

probes: Does a permission change require re-embedding?
How do you prove deletes meet the deadline?
agenda.referenceFix: SLA on delete propagation, priority consumer for tombstones, periodic reconcile job, block erasure completion until index confirms, and monitor lag alerts.

nuggets.title: Historical backfill clobbered live search index

scenario.symptoms: Night backfill job rewrote entire Elasticsearch index using old snapshot, dropping a day of new documents from search.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Backfill pipeline uses same index alias as live writer without isolated rebuild and alias swap.

incident.headline: Backfill wrote directly to live index alias

agenda.goal: Run large imports quickly without hurting live traffic or other tenants.
agenda.opener: Search lost a day of docs after backfill—the indexing path is highlighted. How should backfill run safely?

evidence.strong: Estimates parsing core-hours and embedding GPU-hours from page and chunk counts, runs backfills in separate lower-priority queues, applies per-tenant fair scheduling and quotas, scales workers for the import, and reports progress per tenant.
evidence.adequate: Adds more workers without estimates or isolation.

misconceptions.pattern: Uses the same queue for imports and live updates.
misconceptions.challenge: A new tenant imports ten million documents. What happens to another tenant's edit made a minute later?

probes: Show me rough numbers for parsing and embedding.
How do you keep tenants from starving each other?
hints: Separate bulk work from interactive work.
Pages and chunks drive the bill.
agenda.referenceFix: Build new index offline, dual-write or catch-up delta, atomic alias swap, freeze backfill from touching production alias, and validate doc counts before cutover.

nuggets.title: Zip bomb slipped through ingestion sandbox

scenario.symptoms: Parser cluster outage after nested zip expanded to 800 GB logical size. Antivirus scan skipped for 'trusted' enterprise uploads.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Sandbox trusts tenant flag bypassing depth and compression ratio checks.

incident.headline: Trusted bypass skipped compression bomb checks

agenda.goal: Handle untrusted files and protect tenant data.
agenda.opener: One upload expanded to hundreds of GB—the security scan path is highlighted. How do you contain it?

evidence.strong: Parsers run sandboxed with CPU, memory and time limits; malformed files, zip bombs and macros are contained; repeated failures go to a dead-letter queue with alerts; tenants isolated in storage and indexes; PII detection per tenant policy; documents treated as untrusted content for downstream LLMs.

misconceptions.pattern: Trusts that customer files are well-formed.
misconceptions.challenge: A file decompresses to terabytes. What happens to the parser host?

probes: What happens to a file that crashes the parser every time?
Could text in a document affect the assistants later?
agenda.referenceFix: Always enforce max depth, ratio, and extracted bytes limits, run AV in isolated workers, quota per tenant, and kill switches on anomalous expansion.
